..The upper pattern this morning is defined by a 
high amplitude trough across the West/Great Basin and associated
upper-low centered over northern Nevada, and a high amplitude 
ridge upstream to its west near 135W in the Eastern Pacific. 
Water vapor imagery showing the trough axis extends south 
through southern California toward the SSW. A distinct jet 
streak out ahead of this trough axis extends from the Baja Spur 
NNE into Tucson and up to NW AZ this morning. Given the elevated
precipitable water values from Tucson west (GOES PWATs between 
0.80 and 1.10 inches), this feature is responsible for the 
scattered weak showers flaring up across eastern Pima and 
eastern Pinal county early this morning. These showers will 
continue to translate east this morning and weaken, with the 
trough axis eventually swinging through early this afternoon 
resulting in isolated weak showers. Precipitation with these 
showers are not expected to be impactful, with generally between
a trace to tenth inch expected, and locally heavier amounts up 
to a third inch possible.

The main weather story continues to be a significant easterly
wind event across Southeast Arizona Friday into Saturday.
Forecast models remain in solid agreement with the evolution of
an anomalously strong ridge of high pressure aloft building 
into the Great Basin and northern Intermountain West during the 
latter half of the week. This will drive a strong surface high 
southward along the southern Rockies, resulting in a very tight
pressure gradient across Southeast Arizona. The 13/00Z GFS and
ECMWF ensemble guidance still supports an anomalously strong 
surface high, with sfc pressure on the order of 2.5 to 3.5 
standard deviations above normal. 

What has increased confidence in this wind event is the good
run-to-run consistency in both the strength and persistence
of the lower-level wind. Recent guidance continues to indicate 
850 mb winds of 45-55 kts across southern and eastern portions 
of our CWA between 16/06Z-18Z Friday, with winds remaining
elevated between 40-45 kts through 17/18Z Saturday. This 
prolonged period of strong easterly flow, combined with a very 
tight surface pressure gradient, increases confidence in a 
significant and potentially long-duration wind event across 
Southeast Arizona.

Of particular interest is the forecast vertical stability
profile, with strong static stability near and immediately
above ridge-top level. This, combined with the persistent
strong easterly cross-barrier flow appears favorable for 
mountain-wave development...with potentially significant 
downslope wind acceleration along the lee slopes of the higher 
terrain (west side of the higher terrain in this particular 
case). Although the strongest winds may be focused immediately 
downstream of the higher terrain, terrain gaps and east-west 
oriented valleys will also be susceptible to strong winds given 
the magnitude and duration of the low-level pressure gradient.

Confidence is high that at least Wind Advisory criteria will be
met Friday and Saturday, with sustained ELY/SELY winds of 30-35
mph and gusts of 50-60 mph. However, given the magnitude and 
persistence of the strong winds along with the potential for 
mountain-wave amplification, there is increasing concern that 
portions of the area could experience sustained winds exceeding 
40 mph and gusts in excess of 60 mph. Although confidence in 
advisory-level winds is high, uncertainty remains regarding the 
magnitude and areal extent of the strongest winds. A High Wind 
Watch may become necessary as we get closer to the event and 
confidence in warning-level winds increases.

In any event, given the increasing confidence in a prolonged 
period of advisory-level winds, I decided to issue a Wind 
Advisory early to provide additional lead time for the numerous 
outdoor activities planned across Southeast Arizona this 
weekend. We will continue to closely monitor subsequent model 
runs with regards to the evolution of the low-level winds and 
vertical stability profile to see if we need to address
upgrading wind headlines.
